title: Mullin defends flight as he bears brunt of lawmakers’ ire during threats hearing | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

After an intense week of widespread tech outages and the news of Iran’s plotting to detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, DC, lawmakers pressed top security officials to reassure concerned Americans that there is no ongoing coordinated attack against the homeland.

“We’re 98% confident that there is no nefarious activity going on,” Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin testified about the outages at the annual Worldwide Threats hearing before the House committee on Homeland Security.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified with a “very high level of confidence” that a series of private and government outages in the past week are not the result of a cyberattack. Explaining the analysis, he said that each outage had different root causes and none showed digital hallmarks of an attack.

“They are different causes,” Clayton said. “We have then looked inside the government, inside the private sector … What are the techniques, tactics, and procedures that have been used in the past for that type of (hacking) activity? Do we see any of them here? We do not see them.”

On questions over Iran plotting potential attacks in the US, including over CNN’s reporting that Iran isplotting to detonate a dirty bombin the nation’s capital — with intel remaining unclear on whether the country has the ability or intent to actually do it — Clayton said there was “a suite of threats” focused on mass casualties of civilians “and they have been around for a long time.”

Clayton added the US faces a “heightened threat from the Iranians” and that Iran has demonstrated “a network capability that is very sophisticated, global, and one that we need to combat seriously and with all the tools we have available.”

Aside from the concerns of recent days, the lawmakers also pressed the officials on the oversight of their respective agencies, President Donald Trump’s involvement in decision making, and how ICE agents are trained.

Mullin, who bore the brunt of lawmakers’ ire Thursday, was attacked over his decision to fly in a government plane to a Saturday college football game as the country was still reeling from an air traffic control outage that caused a nationwide ground stop of all flights.

“We had deep conversations about it, and it came in that if we cancel something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there,” Mullin argued over his choice to attend the LSU-Texas game in Louisiana.

“I was meeting other people there. That would show distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” he said, noting he reimbursed the government for the flight, which was on a government plane due to the requirements of his job.

Mullin was also pressed on the decision of his predecessor — former Secretary Kristi Noem — to cut training for new Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits amid a surge in hiring.

“A lot of these decisions were made prior to me coming to office,” Mullin testified, adding that the past training standards have been restored. “We changed a lot of things when we came in. I can’t answer to the previous administration.”

The cuts, according to CNN reporting, resulted in a period of minimal background checks of new officers. Mullin said ICE officers conducting arrests have undergone full background checks and that officers who have not completed the training “have been put on administrative leave until that happens.”

Mullin also weaved around questions about the status of investigations into the ICE officers who shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti, instead firing back that undocumented immigrants have also killed US citizens.

“I cannot talk about ongoing investigations,” Mullin said before immediately switching to lives lost at “the hands of illegals.”

“Does that justify the killing” of Good and Pretti, Democratic Rep. Pablo Hernandez shot back. “And why do you have to bring up that comparison? That is very disrespectful to those people.”

FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia, a stand-in for Director Kash Patel, said emphatically during the hearing that President Donald Trump hasn’t directed the FBI to conduct investigations.

“Are you aware of any instance where the president has directed the FBI to investigate or not investigate anyone?” Democratic Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson asked.

“Absolutely not,” Raia replied.

The answer, however, does not account for the myriad of social media posts from Trump calling for investigations and charges against his perceived enemies, some of which, including cases against former FBI Director James Comey, were later launched.

Raia’s answer is similarly undermined by testimony from one of his own agents in late October.

Earlier this month, a federal judge dismissed a case against two former FBI officials accused of lying about their knowledge of Hunter Biden’s laptop in part because of an FBI agent’s testimony on how the investigation began with public calls from Trump.

According to testimony from the agent, the investigation into former officials and others began after Trump, in a public address this summer, called for those agents to be investigated on a different matter.

The next day, the agent testified, Patel asked for the FBI to investigate those former officials and listed off potential conspiracy charges. The charges Patel had sought, however, were never pursued because of a lack of evidence, the agent testified.

The agent said the investigation was seen by other agents in his field office as a “witch hunt.”

The judge dismissed the case finding that there was no probable cause showing the agents lied and, in several instances, noted that claims prosecutors argued were untrue were, in fact, accurate.

In opening Wednesday’s hearing, Republican Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino lambasted Patel for not attending the hearing Wednesday.

“I am disappointed that Director Patel chose not to appear before the committee today,” Garbarino said, noting that the date of the hearing was given to Patel in August.

The Republican chairman noted that Patel’s refusal to testify is a “significant departure from well-established committee precedent” and that his required attendance on a hearing over worldwide threats “transcends politics, and the director should be here to brief Congress.”

The FBI notified the committee that Raia would be testifying during today’s hearing weeks ago, according to one official, adding that Patel had several meetings with law enforcement across the country scheduled this week.
